title: Polycarp
hookLine: asked to curse Christ, the old bishop says he's served him eighty-six years and he's done no wrong

cards: Soldiers arrive at a farmhouse outside Smyrna late in the evening. The man they've come for could have run again. He doesn't.
He comes downstairs, talks with them, and, according to the account written by his church, orders food and drink set out for them, as much as they want. Then he asks one thing: time to pray.
They give it, and he prays so long, and so fully, that some of the men who came to arrest him are sorry they came. His name is Polycarp. He is the bishop of Smyrna, and he is very old.

teach.b: The Martyrdom of Polycarp is a letter from his church telling what happened. In the stadium the crowd is roaring. The proconsul, the Roman governor, is almost gentle.
Have respect for your age, he says. Swear by the fortune of Caesar. Say: away with the atheists.

That's what the crowd called Christians, because they wouldn't honor the gods. Polycarp looks up at the packed stands, waves his hand at the crowd, groans, looks to heaven, and says: away with the atheists.
He says the words and turns them around. The governor presses: swear, and I'll let you go; curse Christ.

teach.h: EIGHTY-SIX YEARS I HAVE SERVED HIM.
teach.b: And Polycarp answers, in the line the church remembered: eighty-six years I have served him, and he has done me no wrong. How can I blaspheme my King who saved me?
Some take eighty-six years as his age, others as the years since his baptism. Either way, a lifetime. The governor threatens wild beasts, then fire.

teach.h: FIRE THAT BURNS A LITTLE WHILE.
teach.b: Polycarp answers that the governor's fire burns for a little while and goes out. The account says the fire was lit around him, and in the end an executioner's dagger took his life.

teach.h: HIS DEATH KEPT AS A BIRTHDAY.
teach.b: Then a very human detail: his church gathered his bones, laid them somewhere safe, and planned to gather there to keep the day of his death as a birthday. Tradition says Polycarp had known John, the disciple of Jesus.
That ties him to this week's road: Peter and Paul, Luke, the Didache, Clement's plea, Ignatius. Polycarp had even received a letter from Ignatius himself.

how: Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican churches remember Polycarp as a saint and martyr on his feast day, and the Martyrdom of Polycarp is read as an early example of Christians keeping the anniversary of a martyr's death.

games.q: you're Polycarp in the stadium. the governor says: swear by Caesar, say 'away with the atheists,' and go home. what do you do?
o: say it, and mean it as the governor means it.
say it, but wave at the crowd as you do.
games.why: he looks at the crowd, waves his hand, and says away with the atheists, turning the words around. then he refuses to curse Christ.

practice: Bring to mind someone you've been faithful to for years, a spouse, a friend, a parent, a child, a congregation, a promise, and roughly count the years: the good, the dull, the hard.
Then turn it around, and name someone who has been faithful to you. If you pray, give thanks to God for them and for whatever has kept you faithful; if you don't, simply let gratitude sit with you.

wordCard.voice: Polycarp. The old bishop of Smyrna who, told to curse Christ, said he had served him eighty-six years and had never been wronged.

orig.note: Greek: away with the atheists, the cry the governor tells Polycarp to say (Martyrdom of Polycarp 9).

carryVoice: Your line: eighty-six years. A lifetime, said in one sentence. Day seven hundred fifty-six, and counting.
